newsitem.title: FRANCE: Summary of French Socialists economic policies.
newsitem.headline: Summary of French Socialists economic policies.

text.p: The following is a summary of preliminary economic proposals of the opposition Socialist party, presented by party leader Lionel Jospin.
-- The emphasis is on boosting growth, by raising demand via an increase in purchasing power through carefully regulated, non-inflationary rises in salaries.

-- The party is committed to launching a single European currency, though Jospin has said he is against new austerity measures to meet a strict interpretation of a Maastricht treaty criterion setting a ceiling on budget deficits of three percent of gross domestic product. It wants Italy, Spain and Portugal in European monetary union at the start.
It made the following specific proposals to boost demand, growth and jobs in a statement released on March 18:

1) Eliminate payroll charges for health care and replace them with a new health tax applied to all forms of income within two years. This would go significantly further than an existing government measure to shift the cost of health care off payroll charges.

2) Reduce the working week to 35 hours in two steps over the next two to three years without cutting pay. This would involve passing a law setting a 35-hour legal limit to the work week, putting in place means to force employers to observe the limit, and creating financial incentives to encourage employers to further cut the work week.
3) Create 700,000 jobs for the young. Half in the public sector and half in the private sector.
Those in the public sector would be created over the next two years by means of a five-year job contract for 18-25 year olds that would replace over time all other youth employment initiatives.
The state would pay for these contracts without increasing overall public spending by shifting money from other job creation initiatives.
The Socialists would rely mostly on a sense of "moral obligation" by companies for the 350,000 private sector jobs.
4) Encourage early retirement of about 200,000 employees with 40 years on the job to make room for younger, cheaper workers to get permanent jobs.
If totally successful, the measure would cost about eight billion francs a year for five years. It could be financed in part by companies paying less for the new workers.
